tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the README tables match a public harness pair in the repo, examples/echo_server/main.cpp + examples/echo_client/main.cpp (uv-cpp) versus examples/boost_asio_echo_server/main.cpp + examples/boost_asio_echo_client/main.cpp (Boost.Asio), both servers printing received kbyte/s exactly as the README and the chart axes ('K byte/sec', 'one client ping-pong', 'concurrency client ping-pong') report, and the README states gcc 8.3.0, '-O2', libuv 1.30.0 (vendored in the repo), Boost.Asio 1.67 and an Intel Core i5-8265U. Packet size and client count are hard-coded constants that must be edited per table cell, and each figure is a single one-second printout with no repeats.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README tables, kbyte/s received by the echo server (uv-cpp vs boost.asio 1.67), one client: 1K 16138 vs 16119 (+0.1%, derived from page data), 2K 32071 vs 31566 (+1.6%, derived), 4K 59264 vs 58322 (+1.6%, derived), 8K 123813 vs 126210 (-1.9%, derived: Asio faster). 4K packets with N clients: 10 654282 vs 633818 (+3.2%, derived), 100 591869 vs 585716 (+1.1%, derived), 1000 401500 vs 371386 (+8.1%, derived), 5000 412855 vs 382402 (+8.0%, derived). Apache bench HTTP screenshots (1000 concurrency, 100000 requests; images in wlgq2/uv_cpp_res/vs_nginx): uv-cpp 15408.06 req/s (6.490 s, 0 failed, 56-byte /hello.html) vs nginx 1.14.2 16945.71 req/s (5.901 s, 512 failed requests, 13-byte /hello.html), so uv-cpp is about 9% slower than nginx (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Loopback TCP ping-pong echo between a client and a server process on one machine, throughput as kbyte/s received by the server (one-second timer printout), at 1K/2K/4K/8K bytes per packet with one client and with 10/100/1000/5000 clients at 4K bytes; uv-cpp (libuv 1.30.0 wrapper) echo_server/echo_client against a Boost.Asio 1.67 echo server/client written in the same style. A second comparison runs Apache bench (1000 concurrency, 100000 requests, /hello.html) against uv-cpp's HTTP server and nginx 1.14.2.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark harness is public but not parameterized: examples/echo_client/main.cpp hard-codes a 4096-byte message and 1 client, examples/boost_asio_echo_client/main.cpp hard-codes 8192 bytes and 1 client, so each README cell needs a constant edited; each number is one one-second printout with no repeat count or variance, on a 4-core laptop CPU (i5-8265U) with client and server sharing the machine, so the 0.1% to 8% gaps are within plausible run-to-run noise. uv-cpp is slower at 8K packets (-1.9%) and slower than nginx 1.14.2 on the HTTP test (15408 vs 16946 req/s, about 9% slower; the two servers also returned different documents, 56 vs 13 bytes, and nginx had 512 failed requests). Harness asymmetry: the uv-cpp echo writes straight from its libuv read buffer with no copy (TcpConnection::write passes the pointer to uv_write), while the Asio harness std::copies each read into a separate 32 KB write buffer and uses async_write_some (a short write would silently drop bytes). The README numbers date from about April 2020 (echo_client was added 2020-04-18); TcpConnection.cpp received further 'fix bug', 'cycle buffer' and 'time wheel' commits in July-December 2020, so the measured code is not pinned to a commit. Boost.Asio 1.67 and nginx 1.14.2 are old (2018). The examples/pingpang program (packet-framed, message count per second) is not the source of the tables. The comparison is libuv wrapper versus Asio and nginx, not a C++ standard-library facility. Last commit 2025-11-13 is a README edit; the last code change is 2023-12-23 ('fix http send').

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match the README exactly; the nginx screenshots are readable and show uv-cpp about 9% slower than nginx, which the record omitted, so the entry is essentially a tie with Boost.Asio rather than a clear win (record as a 'not clearly faster' shortcoming, not a reject). The record's caveat pointed at examples/pingpang as the harness; the real harness is the echo_server/echo_client pair, which makes the benchmark reproducible with constant edits, hence the upgrade to A.
